subject: religious-studies
topicDisplay: Study Of Religion Christianity Islam Buddhism Hinduism Judaism Sikhism
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Calvin's 'sensus divinitatis' refers to:
options: The sixth sacrament of the church
An innate awareness or sense of the divine implanted in all people
A proof of God derived from cosmic motion
The hierarchy of angels in heaven
questions.explain: Calvin's sensus divinitatis is the inborn sense or awareness of God he believed exists in every human being.

questions.q: Which biblical narrative does Augustine treat as the origin of original sin?
options: The Tower of Babel
The Exodus from Egypt
The Fall of Adam and Eve in Genesis 3
The Flood and Noah's ark
questions.explain: Augustine grounded original sin in the disobedience of Adam and Eve recounted in Genesis 3.

questions.q: Understanding Jesus as 'liberator' stresses that he:
options: Sought purely individual, inward salvation only
Challenged oppression and proclaimed freedom for the marginalised and poor
Endorsed the existing social hierarchy without question
Avoided all conflict with political authorities
questions.explain: The liberator model highlights Jesus' challenge to injustice and his concern for the poor and oppressed.

questions.q: For Augustine, the doctrine of original sin teaches that human sinfulness is:
options: Inherited by all humanity as a consequence of the Fall of Adam
Confined to those who consciously reject God's grace
A learned behaviour acquired through social corruption alone
An illusion created by the limitations of human reason
questions.explain: Augustine held that original sin is transmitted to all humanity through Adam's first sin at the Fall.

questions.q: Presenting Jesus as a 'teacher of wisdom' emphasises his role in:
options: Offering moral and spiritual teaching, e.g. in the Sermon on the Mount and parables
Writing the books of the New Testament himself
Leading an armed political revolt
Performing administrative duties in the Temple
questions.explain: As a teacher of wisdom, Jesus is seen primarily through his ethical and spiritual teaching, such as the parables and Sermon on the Mount.

questions.q: Liberation theology characteristically uses which tool to analyse social injustice?
options: Aristotelian metaphysics
Kantian deontology
Cartesian doubt
A Marxist analysis of economic structures and class oppression
questions.explain: Liberation theology draws on Marxist social and economic analysis to expose structures of oppression.

questions.q: Revealed theology, by contrast, claims that knowledge of God comes chiefly through:
options: Empirical scientific investigation
Innate human intuition unaided by God
God's self-disclosure, supremely in scripture and Christ
Philosophical proofs alone
questions.explain: Revealed theology holds that genuine knowledge of God depends on God's revelation, above all in scripture and Jesus Christ.

questions.q: The 'preferential option for the poor' in liberation theology means that:
options: The poor deserve their poverty as divine punishment
God and the Church should stand especially with the poor and oppressed
Only the wealthy can attain salvation
Poverty should be ignored as a purely economic issue
questions.explain: The preferential option for the poor expresses God's and the Church's special solidarity with the poor and marginalised.

questions.q: The Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark and Luke) are so called because they:
options: Were written by the same single author
Share a similar structure and much common material, allowing parallel viewing
Contain no overlapping content
Were the last gospels to be composed
questions.explain: 'Synoptic' means 'seen together', reflecting the shared structure and parallel material of Matthew, Mark and Luke.

questions.q: 'Universalism' regarding salvation is the view that:
options: Ultimately all people will be reconciled to God and saved
Only a fixed number of the elect will be saved
Hell is eternal for the majority of humanity
Salvation is impossible without church membership
questions.explain: Universalism is the belief that God's salvation will eventually embrace all people.

questions.q: Rosemary Radford Ruether, unlike Daly, generally argued that:
options: Patriarchy is divinely ordained
Christianity is wholly irredeemable for women
Feminism and theology are incompatible
Christianity can be reformed and contains liberating resources for women
questions.explain: Ruether sought to reform Christianity from within, holding it contains liberating resources, whereas Daly ultimately rejected it.

questions.q: In Christian ethics, appealing to 'the Church' as a source of moral authority means relying on:
options: The collective teaching, tradition and magisterium of the Christian community
Scientific consensus
The private judgement of each individual
Government legislation
questions.explain: The Church as a moral source refers to the community's shared teaching, tradition, and (for Catholics) the magisterium.

questions.q: Bonhoeffer's notion of 'costly grace' is contrasted with:
options: Predestination
Cheap grace, which offers forgiveness without discipleship or repentance
Natural law ethics
Works righteousness alone
questions.explain: Bonhoeffer opposed 'costly grace', which demands discipleship, to 'cheap grace', which claims forgiveness without commitment or repentance.

questions.q: In Christian thought, conscience as a guide to moral action is often understood as:
options: Identical to obeying civil law
An infallible inner voice that can never err
A faculty for discerning right and wrong, which may need formation
A purely emotional reaction with no moral content
questions.explain: Conscience is widely seen as a moral faculty that must be informed and formed, rather than an automatically infallible voice.

questions.q: According to Augustine, before the Fall the relationship between Adam and Eve was characterised chiefly by:
options: Domination of one over the other
Fear of divine punishment
Lust and rivalry
Friendship and harmonious mutual love
questions.explain: Augustine taught that pre-Fall human relationships were marked by friendship and ordered love, disrupted only after the Fall.

questions.q: For Calvin, the natural human knowledge of God is rendered ineffective for salvation because:
options: God has hidden himself entirely from creation
Reason has no role whatsoever in religion
Human sin distorts and suppresses the sensus divinitatis
Nature contains no evidence of a designer
questions.explain: Calvin argued that sin corrupts and suppresses the innate sense of God, so saving knowledge requires grace and revelation.

questions.q: Bonhoeffer's commitment to civil disobedience was expressed in his:
options: Withdrawal from all political concern
Support for the Nazi regime's policies
Endorsement of the German state church's compromise
Active resistance to Nazism, including involvement in plots against Hitler
questions.explain: Bonhoeffer opposed the Nazi regime and joined the resistance, including conspiracy against Hitler, exemplifying costly discipleship.

questions.q: Within natural theology, the role of grace is often understood as:
options: Wholly unnecessary if reason functions correctly
A reward strictly earned by intellectual effort
Completing and perfecting what reason can only begin to grasp
Opposed to all use of human reason
questions.explain: Many theologians hold that grace perfects and completes the partial knowledge of God available to natural reason.

questions.q: The claim that Jesus is the 'Son of God' in Christian doctrine asserts that he is:
options: A created angelic being
One god among many in a pantheon
An exalted human prophet only
Divine, sharing in the nature of God
questions.explain: Calling Jesus the Son of God affirms his divinity and shared nature with God the Father.

questions.q: For Bonhoeffer, true discipleship requires:
options: Concrete obedience and willingness to follow Christ even at great cost
Avoidance of all suffering
Strict separation of faith from the world
Comfortable acceptance of grace without obedience
questions.explain: Bonhoeffer taught that genuine discipleship means costly, concrete obedience to Christ, even to the point of suffering.

questions.q: The Christian doctrine of purgatory traditionally refers to:
options: The final destruction of the unsaved
The immediate entry of all souls into heaven
A state of purification for the saved before fully entering heaven
The bodily resurrection at the end of time
questions.explain: Purgatory is understood as an intermediate state in which the saved are purified before fully entering heaven.

questions.q: The concept of the 'imago Dei' teaches that human beings are:
options: Reincarnated divine spirits
Wholly identical in nature to God
Created in the image and likeness of God
Merely advanced animals with no spiritual nature
questions.explain: The imago Dei is the doctrine that humans are made in the image of God, grounding their dignity and capacity for relationship with him.

questions.q: For Augustine, the highest human good and the goal of the will is:
options: The acquisition of earthly wisdom
Political stability in the earthly city
Freedom from all bodily desire
The summum bonum, the love and enjoyment of God
questions.explain: For Augustine the summum bonum is God, whom the rightly ordered will loves and enjoys above all else.

questions.q: Inclusivism, as in the idea of the 'anonymous Christian', maintains that:
options: All religions are equally false
Salvation is impossible outside Christianity
Non-Christians may be saved through Christ even without explicit Christian faith
Only baptised church members can be saved
questions.explain: Inclusivism teaches that the saving work of Christ can reach sincere people of other faiths, sometimes called 'anonymous Christians'.

questions.q: John Hick's pluralism employs which famous analogy to describe the religions?
options: A potter shaping clay
Different paths up the same mountain, with God as the common ultimate reality
The watch and the watchmaker
The cave and its shadows
questions.explain: Hick's pluralism likens the religions to different culturally conditioned responses to one ultimate divine Reality.

questions.q: In the theology of religions, 'exclusivism' is the view that:
options: All religions lead equally to salvation
God's existence cannot be known at all
Salvation is found only through explicit faith in Christ
Non-Christians are saved by sincere following of their own faith
questions.explain: Exclusivism holds that salvation comes only through explicit faith in Jesus Christ.

questions.q: Augustine used the term 'concupiscence' primarily to describe:
options: The divine grace that heals fallen nature
Disordered desire that resists the rule of reason and will
The original harmony of Adam before the Fall
The rational ordering of the will toward God
questions.explain: Concupiscence is Augustine's term for the disordered, uncontrollable desire afflicting fallen human nature.

questions.q: The doctrine of 'limited election' (limited atonement) holds that:
options: Salvation depends entirely on human free choice
God elects new people in every generation by lottery
Christ's saving work is effective only for the elect chosen by God
Everyone will ultimately be saved regardless of faith
questions.explain: Limited election teaches that Christ's atonement is intended and effective only for a particular elect group.

questions.q: Some theologians interpret heaven and hell symbolically rather than literally, meaning they are understood as:
options: Temporary holding places before reincarnation
Political descriptions of just and unjust societies
Physical locations above and below the earth
States of being in relationship with or alienation from God
questions.explain: A symbolic reading treats heaven and hell as states of communion with or separation from God rather than physical places.

questions.q: Hick proposed a 'Copernican revolution' in theology, meaning a shift from:
options: Faith to reason
A God-centred to a humanity-centred view
A Christianity-centred to a God- or Reality-centred view of the religions
Scripture to tradition
questions.explain: Hick called for moving Christianity from the centre to placing the ultimate divine Reality at the centre, with all faiths revolving around it.
